title: STACK: Build a Personal Operating System That Survives Real Life
description: You don't have a motivation problem. You have a design problem. Everybody's got a plan until life hits them in the mouth — a knee gives out, a bill shows up, a kid gets sick, a deadline moves. Then the workout gets skipped, the budget falls apart, the side hustle eats the semester, and you're back to promising yourself you'll try harder next time. STACK isn't another book telling you to wake up at 5 a.m. and want it more. It's a five-part system — See, Triage, Architect, Cycle, Keep Learning — built by an engineer in his fifties who ran out of patience for advice that only works if you're twenty-two with nothing on your plate yet. You'll watch it get built in real time through Daniel, a guy trying to rebuild a life that's already gotten complicated, and Joseph, a guy trying to build one before it does. This book won't hand you a perfect routine. Nobody's life survives one of those past the second bad week. It'll hand you something better — a system that bends instead of breaking, tells you what to cut when everything can't fit, and gets you back on your feet fast when it inevitably falls apart anyway. Because it will fall apart. That was never the part you could control. Read it once for the framework. title: Stacked: The No-BS System to Stack Skills, Build Leverage, and Become Unstoppable
description: Most people believe reinvention requires starting over. New credentials. A clean slate. A leap of faith. STACKED dismantles that myth. This book is a practical, unsentimental system for turning the life you’ve already lived into leverage, by identifying, combining, and compounding skills you didn’t even realize you were building. It’s written for people who feel capable but stuck, experienced but undervalued, or resilient enough to survive change but unsure how to turn that resilience into momentum. Through a clear four-stage triage framework, readers learn how to accurately assess where they are, crisis, depletion, stagnation, or optimization, and why applying the wrong strategy at the wrong time keeps people spinning. From there, the book moves into skill inventory: uncovering raw, mid-tier, and premium skills forged through work, setbacks, side paths, and survival itself. The stories range from door-knocking real estate grind and sleeping in cars, to scaling a multi-cast entertainment company, to rebuilding income and identity when entire industries collapse overnight. Each chapter shows how skills transfer across domains, how unrelated experiences quietly train leadership, sales, systems thinking, and emotional regulation, and how those skills compound when intentionally stacked. This is a blueprint for becoming antifragile: building a life and career that get stronger under pressure instead of breaking. title: The Innovation Stack: Building an Unbeatable Business One Crazy Idea at a Time
description: From the cofounder of Square, an inspiring and entertaining account of what it means to be a true entrepreneur and what it takes to build a resilient, world-changing company In 2009, a St. Louis glassblowing artist and recovering computer scientist named Jim McKelvey lost a sale because he couldn't accept American Express cards. Frustrated by the high costs and difficulty of accepting credit card payments, McKelvey joined his friend Jack Dorsey (the cofounder of Twitter) to launch Square, a startup that would enable small merchants to accept credit card payments on their mobile phones. With no expertise or experience in the world of payments, they approached the problem of credit cards with a new perspective, questioning the industry's assumptions, experimenting and innovating their way through early challenges, and achieving widespread adoption from merchants small and large. But just as Square was taking off, Amazon launched a similar product, marketed it aggressively, and undercut Square on price. For most ordinary startups, this would have spelled the end. Instead, less than a year later, Amazon was in retreat and soon discontinued its service. How did Square beat the most dangerous company on the planet? Was it just luck? These questions motivated McKelvey to study what Square had done differently from all the other companies Amazon had killed. He eventually found the key: a strategy he calls the Innovation Stack. McKelvey's fascinating and humorous stories of Square's early days are blended with historical examples of other world-changing companies built on the Innovation Stack to reveal a pattern of ground-breaking, competition-proof entrepreneurship that is rare but repeatable. title: The Great Game of Business, Expanded and Updated: The Only Sensible Way to Run a Company
description: In the early 1980s, Springfield Remanufacturing Corporation (SRC) in Springfield, Missouri, was a near bankrupt division of International Harvester. That's when a green young manager, Jack Stack, took over and turned it around. He didn't know how to "manage" a company, but he did know about the principal, of athletic competition and democracy: keeping score, having fun, playing fair, providing choice, and having a voice. With these principals he created his own style of management -- open-book management. The key is to let everyone in on financial decisions. At SRC, everyone learns how to read a P&L -- even those without a high school education know how much the toilet paper they use cuts into profits. SRC people have a piece of the action and a vote in company matters. Imagine having a vote on your bonus and on what businesses the company should be in. SRC restored the dignity of economic freedom to its people. Stack's "open-book management" is the key -- a system which, as he describes it here, is literally a game , and one so simple anyone can use it. As part of the Currency paperback line, the book includes a "User's Guide" -- an introduction and discussion guide created for the paperback by the author -- to help readers make practical use of the book's ideas. Jack Stack is the president and CEO of the Springfield Remanufacturing Corporation, in Springfield, Missouri. title: Hedge Your Stack: Gold & Silver Perpetual Futures for Stackers — Leverage, Funding, Liquid
description: Every perps explainer repeats the same rule: at 5x leverage it takes a 20% move to wipe you out. On Kalshi, the US exchange where traders can now take leveraged positions in gold and silver perpetual futures, that rule is badly wrong. The author typed positions into the exchange's own order ticket and read the liquidation price it showed: a 5x long liquidated about 8% from entry, not 20%. A 10x gold long, about 5%. At gold's 15x maximum, a move of about 1% ends the trade. Hedge Your Stack is a short, numbers-first field guide for people who already own physical gold and silver (stackers, flippers and resellers) and want to understand the leveraged perps that now trade next to it, 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Inside: Where the liquidation price really sits, with calibrated tables for gold and silver from 2x to 15x What funding costs to hold a position, and why it is charged on the full position, not your margin How a 1x short perp hedges metal you already hold, over a weekend or while you wait to sell, with two worked examples The event contracts and 15-minute markets on the same metals, and what they can and can't insure A checklist to tape next to your monitor before you click Every number is dated, and every chapter ends with a "Live now" link to a page that keeps it current. Not investment, tax or legal advice. Perpetual futures carry leverage and can lose your entire margin quickly.
